stem:
An emergency registrar assesses a 58-kg adult who has taken immediate-release paracetamol 1.5 g every four hours while awake, about 7.5 g/day, for three days of dental pain. The last dose was six hours ago; there is nausea but no shock or known liver disease. Paracetamol is 16 mg/L and ALT is 180 U/L (reference <40); the Poisons Information Centre is being contacted.

Which treatment decision is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Plot the level at six hours and withhold treatment if below the line
options.explanation: The nomogram is not valid for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion over several days. Timing from the last dose would conceal the earlier exposure and liver injury.

options.label: B
options.text: Withhold acetylcysteine because the concentration is below 20 mg/L
options.explanation: An abnormal ALT following this repeated exposure is a treatment indication even when the concentration is below that threshold.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the paracetamol level in four hours before deciding
options.explanation: A repeat level adds nothing here: after repeated supratherapeutic ingestion an ALT above 50 U/L already indicates acetylcysteine, so waiting only delays treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: Give activated charcoal and repeat ALT the next day
options.explanation: Charcoal does not treat established liver injury from repeated doses over several days and is not an alternative to indicated acetylcysteine.

options.label: E
options.text: Start acetylcysteine using the repeated-ingestion pathway
options.explanation: Repeated dosing plus elevated ALT warrants acetylcysteine and toxicology-guided monitoring. This decision does not depend on plotting the final dose on an acute-ingestion nomogram.

context: Repeated supratherapeutic paracetamol ingestion is assessed using the exposure pattern and laboratory evidence of injury, not the acute-ingestion nomogram.
